buildNotes: Template rules (2026-10-09): step names are Watch/Explore/Understand/Practice/Apply/Review everywhere. Completion buttons stay disabled until BOTH the practice quiz and exit check are fully answered (solar:quizdone events). Watch prompts must describe the actual embedded clip. The 0.95-1.4 AU classroom zone must never be presented as official - published limits differ, outer edge disputed. Magnetic field = a factor scientists investigate, not a universal requirement. Do not reuse the same interactive twice: L3 = ice thickness or tidal heating (NOT another star-distance slider); L6 = graphs and arithmetic (NOT another essay); L7 competition prep does NOT use this template - mixed questions + binder checklist + timer only after 2027 rules publish. L2 must use the Venus/Earth/Mars contrast, not retell the Venus surprise.

dailyDiscoveries.text: NASA's Spitzer telescope found seven Earth-size planets around one small star, 40 light-years away. Three orbit where liquid water could exist. It's the best nearby laboratory for studying habitability beyond our solar system.
dailyDiscoveries.title: TRAPPIST-1: seven worlds, three in the habitable zone

dailyDiscoveries.text: Saturn's tiny moon Enceladus shoots plumes of salty water from cracks at its south pole — a subsurface ocean venting directly into space, where a spacecraft can fly through and taste it.
dailyDiscoveries.title: Enceladus is spraying its ocean into space

dailyDiscoveries.text: Jupiter's moon Europa hides a global salty ocean beneath its ice shell. Tidal flexing from Jupiter's gravity keeps that water liquid — no sunlight required.
dailyDiscoveries.title: Europa may hold twice Earth's ocean water

dailyDiscoveries.text: Venus is hotter than Mercury even though it's farther from the Sun. Its thick carbon-dioxide atmosphere trapped heat in a runaway greenhouse effect — possibly boiling away an ancient ocean.
dailyDiscoveries.title: Venus: the runaway greenhouse warning

dailyDiscoveries.text: When a planet passes in front of its star, the star dims slightly. That tiny dip — the transit method — has revealed thousands of exoplanets, including most known habitable-zone worlds.
dailyDiscoveries.title: We find exoplanets by watching starlight dip

dailyDiscoveries.text: The James Webb Space Telescope analyzes starlight filtered through exoplanet atmospheres, searching for water vapor, carbon dioxide, and methane — chemical clues about habitability.
dailyDiscoveries.title: JWST is reading exoplanet atmospheres

dailyDiscoveries.text: Dry riverbeds, lake deposits, and minerals that only form in water show Mars was once warm and wet. Today's thin atmosphere can't support liquid water on the surface — but it may survive underground.
dailyDiscoveries.title: Mars once had rivers and lakes
